messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Darius Mensah was 19, African American, and had already started building a life that depended on composure. As a detective, he worked long hours moving between interviews, reports, and late calls, and he had a girlfriend who knew him as steady, observant, hard to shake. That steadiness had been interrupted months earlier when he was held captive in a cramped, windowless place after a case went wrong and he was separated from backup. He remembered the stale air, the hours that stopped meaning anything, the sense that every small sound outside the door could mean he was about to be hurt or moved or forgotten. Even now, he could not tell that story cleanly; he knew what happened, but when he tried to speak about it, the words seemed to disappear, leaving him frustrated and ashamed, as if the event were locked inside him but inaccessible.

The memories did not return in a simple, cinematic way. At times, Darius would feel the full force of what had happened without any clear picture attached to it, a wave of panic and helplessness that seemed to come from nowhere. Other times, a fragment of sound would snap through him—something like the scrape of metal, a muffled shout, the hard echo of footsteps in a corridor—and his mind would briefly fill with the same noises he had heard during captivity. Those moments left him disoriented and angry, because he could not always tell what was memory and what was the present. He had come to dread the experience of remembering at all, not because he wanted to forget everything, but because every attempt to put the event into words seemed to pull him back into the emotion of it, with no relief in sight.

In response, Darius began trying hard not to think about what had happened. He pushed the thoughts away whenever they surfaced, cut off conversations that came too close to the topic, and forced himself to stay busy at work so there would be no empty space for the memories to enter. After dark, he avoided being outside whenever he could. If he had to leave the station late, he would plan his route carefully, keep to well-lit areas, and move quickly from the car to the door without lingering. He told himself night made him vulnerable in a way daylight did not, because the captivity had stripped away his sense of control in the dark, and he did not trust his body to stay calm if he was out there again. He also avoided any form of physical contact with others, even with people he cared about. At home, his girlfriend noticed that he stiffened if she touched his arm unexpectedly, and he would step back with an apology that sounded clipped and overcontrolled.

Over time, these habits narrowed his life. He became more guarded at work, less willing to stay late if it meant leaving after dark, and more likely to hand off tasks that would keep him out in the evening. The avoidance gave him short-term relief, but it also seemed to confirm his fear that the world was a place he could not safely enter unless he stayed vigilant. Because the memories could arrive as sound or raw feeling without warning, he felt he had to keep them suppressed at all costs; if he let himself think about the captivity, he was afraid the same helplessness would flood back and take over the rest of the night. That fear made him increasingly isolated, and his relationship began to carry the strain of his recoil from touch and his refusal to talk about what had happened.

By the time he sought help, Darius was exhausted by how much effort it took to keep himself contained. What finally brought him in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of nights spent scanning every shadow, of silent dinners where he flinched if his girlfriend reached for him, and of workdays spent fighting to hold the memories at bay while they kept returning in fragments of sound and emotion. He was afraid that if he did not get help, he would keep shrinking his world until there was almost nothing left of it. At the same time, he was hoping for a way to tell the story without falling apart, and for a chance to feel close to the people in his life again without his body reacting as if he were still captive.
